extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in security; aspiring security technologists and system/system-designers
extracted.subtask_description: High-level practical guidance for thinking about and designing security: adopt an adversarial mindset, know relevant technologies, observe operational practices, and test systems by trying to break them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Security as a mindset
rubrics_metrics.description: Security is a mindset. It's a way of thinking about systems and how they fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author emphasizes that beyond technical knowledge, security work is primarily about a way of thinking — constantly looking at security systems and how to get around them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the relevant technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Working in security means knowing a lot about technology — computers and networks, cameras and how they work, the chemistry of bomb detection, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers and analysts should have specific technical knowledge relevant to the systems they're protecting so they can understand likely failure modes and attack vectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think like an attacker / adversarial thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Always look for ways a security system fails by imagining how an adversary would defeat it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical advice: if you're hired to build a shoplift-proof store, you should know how to shoplift; if you're designing gait-recognition cameras, anticipate evade techniques. This adversarial mindset informs better defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate simple circumventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Designers must anticipate low-tech or trivial evasion techniques (the example given: people putting rocks in their shoes to defeat gait recognition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete, plausible examples of simple workarounds when threat-modeling a system; build countermeasures for those simple vectors rather than assuming only sophisticated attacks matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Red-team / break-it testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Test security designs by actively trying to break them; understanding attacks informs stronger defenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'cat and mouse' framing: think of security as an adversarial game and practice offensive testing (red-teaming) to reveal weaknesses before real attackers do.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe operational practices for vulnerabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Watch how systems operate in the real world (e.g., restaurant payment flow, bank teller procedures) to find practical vulnerabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational observation yields questions that reveal weak assumptions (e.g., 'If you pay after you eat, why don't more people just leave without paying?') — such questions guide mitigations grounded in actual behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate effectiveness vs displacement
rubrics_metrics.description: When judging a security measure, consider whether it actually prevents harm or merely shifts it elsewhere (e.g., cameras that move crime next door).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the broader system effects and unintended consequences of defenses, not just their localized detection or deterrence capabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical distinction between knowledge and action
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a moral difference between knowing how to defeat a security system and actually using that knowledge to commit wrongdoing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Security professionals should use adversarial knowledge responsibly to improve defenses; the text notes this distinction explicitly to discourage misuse while promoting understanding.
